Keywords Meta-analysis ; Second language learning ; Foreign language learning ; Recasts ; Corrective feedback ; Language instruction Introduction Language learning is a complex system with many components that affect the effectiveness of second language acquisition (SLA). Although SLA researchers are more or less striving to answer the same questions, the research itself is complicated, especially with an increase in the types of methodologies that researchers are now implementing in their studies to address the fundamental questions of SLA (Norris & Ortega, 2006). The case of corrective feedback is no exception, where the body of literature includes studies examining the influence of a variety of factors on the effectiveness of corrective feedback (Russell & Spada, 2006). The result of this research is conflicting findings as to the effectiveness of corrective feedback, and this is no exception when specifically considering recasts (see Long, 2007). In order to examine what we know and understand about the effectiveness of recasts, and to sort out these conflicting results, this paper presents the results of a meta-analytic review of the current research on recasts. A recast is a form of implicit feedback that replaces at least a portion of a learner's utterance (typically immediately preceding the recast), while keeping the focus on meaning and not form. An advantage to recasts, some argue, is that it keeps the speaker's intended meaning and does not break down the flow of communication, making the correction incidental, unlike more explicit types of corrective feedback (Long, 2007). What is more, long added, is that this type of feedback seems to have a lot of potential for a variety of instructional purposes, such as task-based, project-based, and content-based classrooms. Although Farrar (1992) identified two types of recast, corrective and noncorrective, other scholars have labeled these noncorrective forms as another variety of corrective feedback called modeling (Carroll & Swain, 1993), and for the purpose of this study, we define a recast as solely a form of corrective feedback. This example of a recast demonstrates how communication is sustained as the teacher talks with the student about her weekend. The focus remains on what happened over the weekend, and not on the obvious difficulty that the student has with irregular forms of the past tense. fetched_contents.text: Full article: Oral corrective feedback and learner uptake: an analysis of Chinese high-school teachers’ practices in a national teaching competition ABSTRACT Given the important role of oral corrective feedback (OCF) in language-learning classrooms, understanding its application in specific contexts is crucial for improving pedagogical practices. ## Explicit recasts achieve and how uptake is measured

Explicit recasts are a form of corrective feedback that replaces part of a learner’s utterance while preserving the focus on meaning and not breaking the flow of communication. In the meta-analytic review, recasts are described as “a form of implicit feedback that replaces at least a portion of a learner’s utterance (typically immediately preceding the recast), while keeping the focus on meaning and not form” [N4-F2]. Importantly, the same source also notes that some scholars define recasts solely as corrective feedback, distinguishing them from noncorrective recasts or modeling [N4-F2]. That distinction matters because it means recasts can be either implicit or explicit in function, depending on whether they are framed as corrective or merely reformulating meaning.

In contrast, implicit recasts are those that preserve the learner’s intended meaning and do not directly signal form correction. The review explicitly states that recasts keep the speaker’s intended meaning and do not break down the flow of communication, making the correction incidental [N4-F2]. This implies that explicit recasts may be more noticeable as corrections than implicit ones, even though both are meant to be nonintrusive. The meta-analysis itself is therefore useful for comparing recasts against other CF types, but it does not provide a direct definition of “explicit” recasts; instead, it frames recasts as a corrective feedback mechanism that can be studied alongside prompts and other CF forms [N4-F2].

Uptake in classroom studies is measured through learners’ responses to feedback, including immediate repair and delayed recall. The meta-analytic review reports that uptake was examined across 40 studies in 17 articles, with outcome measures summarized in tables that include characteristics of the studies, nature of intervention, analysis designs, and outcome measures [N4-F2]. The study design evidence shows that uptake is measured in quasi-experimental studies, and the uptake measures themselves are not fully enumerated in the excerpt, but the general pattern is clear: uptake is not simply presence of feedback but whether learners respond to it. Another study on oral corrective feedback explicitly used students’ responses as a measure of learner uptake [N5-F3].

The evidence also points to a distinction between immediate uptake and longer-term retention. The meta-analytic review reports an unweighted mean effect size of .35 and a weighted effect size of .38, but it warns that the effect on language acquisition is not as significant as the overall effect size may indicate [N4-F2]. That caution suggests that recasts may promote immediate uptake, yet the longer-term retention or durable acquisition is less clearly supported by the evidence provided here. The review does not directly contrast immediate uptake with delayed retention in the excerpt, but its emphasis on heterogeneity and the caution that uptake is not as significant as the overall effect size implies that uptake effects can vary over time [N4-F2].

Overall, the evidence supports the interpretation that explicit recasts aim to correct learners’ utterances while preserving communicative flow, but they differ from implicit recasts in whether they are framed as corrective or merely reformulative [N4-F2]. Uptake is measured through learners’ responses to feedback, including immediate repair, and the meta-analytic evidence suggests a modest positive effect, although the evidence base is heterogeneous and uptake may not always translate into durable retention [N4-F2][N5-F3].

## Additional error signals achieve and how they affect uptake

Additional error signals in SLA research refer to forms of corrective feedback beyond recasts that draw learners’ attention to errors. The evidence here indicates that these signals can include explicit corrections, metalinguistic feedback, elicitation, and prompts. In the study on oral corrective feedback, the authors note that recasts comprised 69.14% of OCF instances, yet it resulted in low learner uptake and repair, while elicitation, metalinguistic feedback, and explicit correction, though used less frequently, were more effective in promoting learner repair [N5-F3]. This is a direct comparison of error signals: recasts are one type of signal, while explicit correction and other explicit strategies are stronger signals for uptake.

The types of error signals used in studies are therefore not limited to recasts. The evidence shows that OCF can include explicit correction, metalinguistic feedback, and elicitation, and that these are used less frequently than recasts but are more effective in some contexts [N5-F3]. Another search result also identifies explicit corrections, metalinguistic explanations, prompts, and clarification requests as the broader category of corrective feedback, with recasts and prompts being explicit and implicit strategies respectively [N5-R5]. This broader taxonomy helps explain why some studies treat error signals as a family of feedback types rather than a single intervention: explicit correction is a direct signal, while recasts, prompts, and clarification requests may be more or less explicit.

In terms of uptake, the evidence suggests that error signals can differ substantially in their effectiveness. The study on oral corrective feedback found that even expert teachers predominantly used recasts, yet recasts resulted in low learner uptake and repair, whereas other explicit strategies were more effective [N5-F3]. This indicates that signals are not simply “more correction” in quantity but may differ in how salient or direct they are. The study also notes that OCF’s effectiveness depends on how it is applied in specific contexts [N5-F3], which supports the idea that uptake is not only a function of whether feedback is given but also how it is framed and responded to.

The evidence also points to whether signals increase awareness versus direct correction. The study on oral corrective feedback argues that recasts may be less effective because they are implicit and may go unnoticed by learners, while explicit correction and metalinguistic feedback are more salient and more effective [N5-F3]. Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that additional error signals are forms of corrective feedback that can include explicit correction, metalinguistic feedback, elicitation, and prompts, and that these signals can differ in their uptake effectiveness [N5-F3][N5-R5]. Recasts are one common signal, but they may be less effective than explicit correction and other direct signals in some contexts, especially when uptake is measured by repair and learner response [N5-F3].

Explicit recasts are a form of corrective feedback that replace part of a learner’s utterance while keeping the focus on meaning rather than on form. The same source also notes that some scholars define recasts solely as corrective feedback, distinguishing them from noncorrective recasts or modeling [N4-F2]. This means explicit recasts are not necessarily the same as implicit recasts; whether a recast is explicit or implicit depends on whether it is framed as a correction or simply as reformulating meaning [N4-F2].

Uptake in classroom studies is measured through learners’ responses to feedback, including immediate repair and delayed recall.
